description: Solo team led by a plant geneticist and agri-AI developer. Building Rotation Replay: a decision-support tool that replays crop rotations against 40+ years of NASA POWER climate data to show farmers how their rotation would have survived real weather, and which alternatives are more resilient. Not seeking members.
summary: Rotation Replay is a decision-support tool that replays a farmer's crop rotation against the weather that actually happened in every season since 1981, using NASA POWER daily data. Instead of recommending crops from average climate, it shows how often each crop in the rotation would have been stressed by heat, frost, water shortage or harvest rain, whether that is getting worse, and which alternative rotations fit the farmer's priorities for resilience, water, soil health and income. It addresses Field Shift by combining NASA data with soil texture, crop characteristics and farmer priorities. The prototype covers six districts of Punjab, Pakistan.
details:
What it does: the farmer chooses a location, soil texture, irrigation access, a summer (kharif) and winter (rabi) crop, and four priorities. The tool shows (1) a survival record with one cell per season from 1981/82 to 2025/26, (2) the trend in heat days, (3) any season day by day, (4) all 20 rotations ranked by the farmer's priorities, and (5) what a shorter-duration or more heat-tolerant variety, or a new sowing date, would have rescued.

Example: at Sargodha, rice then wheat was stressed in 28 of 90 seasons, 8 of them in the last 15 years. Wheat heat days rose from 3.0 per season (1981-2000) to 5.9 (last 15 years). The 2021/22 wheat season has the most heat days in the record, matching the March 2022 heatwave.

How it works: crop development follows thermal time calibrated at each location. Each season is scored for heat days in the flowering and grain-fill window, frost, the irrigation gap (FAO-56 crop coefficients, Hargreaves evapotranspiration) and rain at harvest. The winter crop is sown only after the summer crop is harvested, so a late crop affects the next one. Soil health uses transparent rules (legumes, crop-family diversity, puddled rice).

Limits: stress scores are screening proxies, not yield predictions. Crop thresholds are editable assumptions. POWER describes district climate (about 50 km), not one field.

Tools: Python, pandas, NumPy, Streamlit, Vega-Lite, GitHub, VS Code.
dataRefs: NASA POWER Project daily point API, agroclimatology community (https://power.larc.nasa.gov): T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN and PRECTOTCORR, 1 January 1981 to 30 June 2026, for six Punjab districts. The data drive crop development, heat and frost day counts, evapotranspiration, irrigation need and harvest-rain risk in every replayed season.
projectRefs: NASA POWER Project (https://power.larc.nasa.gov). Allen et al. (1998), FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56. Open-source software: Python, pandas, NumPy, Streamlit, Vega-Lite. AI assistant: Claude (Anthropic).
